overview: Antekerrepenh, also recorded as Andegerebenha, names an Aboriginal people and an Arandic language associated with country around the Tarlton and Toko ranges and the Field and Hay rivers. Historical descriptions qualify the southern limits of this country. Language names and broad mapping should not be mistaken for the boundaries of a centralized state.

periods.title: Trade in a changing colonial landscape
periods.summary: Roth’s 1897 account describes Toko people exchanging pituri, possum-fibre twine and blankets for goods from neighboring groups. Indigenous trading routes carried introduced goods as well as locally made objects.

periods.title: Speakers contribute recorded knowledge
periods.summary: Recordings made with Tiger George in Boulia preserve documentation of Antekerrepenh vocabulary concerning animals, food, tools, shelter, water and time. The archive identifies both the speaker and recording setting.

periods.title: Kinship distinctions enter linguistic research
periods.summary: Jack Marshall’s explanations helped Gavan Breen recognize a pronoun form associated with brothers-in-law. This contribution showed that social relationships could shape grammatical choices in ways earlier descriptions had missed.

periods.title: Earlier research published as a heritage resource
periods.summary: Breen’s survey of Arandic kinship terminology was published with a 2022 foreword. The work brings together earlier field research; its language-use observations do not constitute a new 2022 census.

items.text: Roth describes people he called Undekerebina traveling from the Toko Ranges to meet Yaroinga traders at Gordon’s Creek or by the Georgina River. They brought pituri, possum-fibre twine and blankets, returning with ochre, boomerangs, stone knives and hair belts. Trade connected different resources and skills.

The same account describes sandstone grinding slabs and handstones made around Walaya and the Toko ranges. Makers cut and shaped stone for movement through regional markets. These tools linked food preparation with skilled manufacture and transport; the regional description does not identify the maker of every surviving specimen.

Roth’s description of an Undekerebina sign for making a net imitates rolling fibre along the thigh while the other hand twists. A sign for wild orange imitates plucking and biting. These recorded gestures connect communication with embodied knowledge of working materials and gathering food.

AIATSIS identifies a July 31, 1970 Boulia recording with Tiger George that covers food plants, tools, fire, clothing and shelter. Its catalogue makes ordinary work visible within the language record. It does not supply a house plan or prove that every listed tool remained in everyday use.

A neighboring recording catalogs Tiger George’s words concerning water, direction and time. The same tape later changes to Pitta Pitta speech by Nora Jacks. Keeping those sections separate prevents knowledge from one language from being assigned to another simply because they share an archival reel.

Bill Jenkin and Jack Marshall contributed plant names and conversation in Antekerrepenh at Dajarra on August 12, 1970. The archive distinguishes their exchange from subsequent Warluwarra recordings on the same reel. Spoken conversation provides a different kind of language record from isolated vocabulary prompted by a researcher.

In 1976, Jack Marshall gave Breen a sentence about addressing two brothers-in-law, then corrected the form the researcher proposed. That correction exposed a grammatical distinction tied to relationships. The example records Marshall’s active role in explaining his language and changing an outside scholar’s analysis.

Breen later found related forms on a recording he had made in 1967 without recognizing their significance. His survey also records variation in how speakers accepted these forms. The resulting analysis is a history of learning and revision, rather than proof that one grammatical rule applied identically everywhere.

AIATSIS catalogs performances and explanations by Didgeroo Jack and Noble Burke that include choruses from marambala, identified as an Antekerrepenh corroboree, alongside Wangkangurru songs. The record shows a multilingual performance setting. The catalogue establishes attribution and context; it does not authorize invented lyrics, meanings or ceremonial details.

Jack Marshall’s Dajarra sessions continued in August 1976, including work on possessive expressions. AIATSIS preserves a sequence of associated recordings, making it possible to trace sustained work with a named contributor. Its finding aid distinguishes permission to listen from conditions governing publication of the audio.

sections.title: Country and the limits of the map

items.text: The AUSTLANG-derived profile links the language to the Field and Hay river region, but explicitly qualifies its southwestern extent and the role of changing flood conditions. This is a reminder that a broad language-area map summarizes relationships with country; it cannot by itself certify a fixed territorial boundary.

ending.text: Andegerebenha remains named among the First Nations whose country is acknowledged by James Cook University’s regional health centre. Language loss and archival preservation are separate from the existence of a people and their connections to country. The imported map ending in 1815 records neither a verified conquest nor extinction.
